9.1 What is Light? Nature & Rectilinear Propagation (Pages 134–135)

We see a rich variety of objects in the world around us. In a pitch-dark room, however, nothing is visible. Upon lighting a candle or bulb, things become visible. What makes things visible? An object reflects the light that falls upon it. When this reflected light enters our eyes, it stimulates the retina and enables our brain to see the object.

1 Light travels in straight lines (Rectilinear propagation)
2 Speed in vacuum: c = 3 × 108 m s-1
3 Casts sharp shadows of opaque obstacles

The straight-line path of light is conventionally represented by a ray of light with an arrow showing its direction of propagation. A collection of such rays forms a beam of light.

🤔 More to Know — Wave vs. Particle Nature: If an opaque object on the path of light becomes extremely tiny, light has a tendency to bend slightly around it instead of travelling in a straight line — an effect known as diffraction. While classical ray optics treats light as straight rays, modern Quantum Theory of Light reconciles the wave theory and particle theory, treating light as discrete packets of energy called photons.

✨

9.2 Fundamental Laws of Reflection of Light (Page 135)

Reflection of light occurs whenever a light ray strikes a boundary and rebounds into the original medium. All reflecting surfaces — plane mirrors, polished metals, water surfaces, and curved mirrors — obey two universal laws:

📜 The Two Universal Laws of Reflection:

  1. First Law: The angle of incidence (∠i) is always equal to the angle of reflection (∠r):
    ∠i = ∠r
  2. Second Law: The incident ray, the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray, all lie in the same plane.
🪞 Plane Mirror Images:
  • Image is always virtual and erect.
  • Size of image is equal to size of object (h' = h).
  • Image distance equals object distance (v = u behind mirror).
  • Image is laterally inverted (left appears right).
🔮 Curved / Spherical Mirrors:
  • Reflecting surface is curved inward or outward.
  • Can form real or virtual images depending on distance.
  • Can magnify, diminish, or produce same-sized images.
  • Still strictly obeys ∠i = ∠r at every local point!

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.1 • Curved Surfaces of a Shining Spoon (NCERT Page 134–135)

  • Take a large, shining stainless steel spoon. Try to view your face in its curved surface.
  • Do you get the image? Is it smaller or larger?
  • Move the spoon slowly away from your face. Observe the image. How does it change?
  • Reverse the spoon and repeat the activity with the outer curved surface. How does the image look now?
  • Compare the characteristics of the images on the two surfaces.
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

1. Inner Curved Surface (Concave): When held close, it forms an erect and enlarged (magnified) virtual image. As the spoon is moved farther away, the image becomes inverted and appears diminished.

2. Outer Curved Surface (Convex): Always forms an erect and diminished (smaller) virtual image, regardless of how far the spoon is moved away. The field of view is wide.

💡 Key Takeaway: The inner curved surface behaves like a concave mirror, while the outer bulging surface behaves like a convex mirror.

🔍

9.3 Types of Spherical Mirrors: Concave vs. Convex (Pages 135–136)

The curved surface of a shining spoon considered in Activity 9.1 is an everyday analogue of a curved mirror. The most common type of curved mirror is the spherical mirror. The reflecting surface of such mirrors can be considered to form a part of the surface of a hollow glass sphere.

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.1: Schematic Representation of Spherical Mirrors (Page 135)

  • 🔹 Concave Mirror [Fig. 9.1(a)]: A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves inward (faces toward the centre of the sphere), producing inner-surface reflection.
  • 🔹 Convex Mirror [Fig. 9.1(b)]: A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves outward (bulges towards the viewer), producing outer-surface reflection.
  • 🔹 Non-Reflecting Silvered Backing: The shaded slanting lines represent the opaque protective silvered paint on the non-reflecting rear side of the glass.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 135):

"Fig. 9.1 — Schematic representation of spherical mirrors; the shaded side is non-reflecting."

🖼️ Fig. 9.1 – Schematic Representation of Spherical Mirrors

📖 Source: NCERT Page 135

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.1 • Schematic Representation of Spherical Mirrors

Q1: Identify which side reflects light in a concave mirror versus a convex mirror.

✅ Answer In a concave mirror, reflection occurs from the inner hollow surface. In a convex mirror, reflection occurs from the outer bulging surface.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (0.5M concave + 0.5M convex)

Q2: What do the shaded slanting lines indicate on the back of each mirror?

✅ Answer The shaded slanting lines indicate the non-reflecting silvered backing (opaque protective coating).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (correct identification of silvered non-reflecting backing)

Q3: How does the curvature of a spoon relate to the two types of mirrors shown in Figure 9.1?

✅ Answer The inner curved cavity acts as a concave mirror, while the outer bulging back acts as a convex mirror.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (identifies inner as concave and outer as convex)

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.2: Geometric Anatomy & Parameters of Spherical Mirrors (Page 135–136)

  • 🔹 Pole (P): The geometric midpoint of the reflecting surface lying directly on the mirror, acting as the coordinate origin (0, 0).
  • 🔹 Centre of Curvature (C): The centre of the hollow sphere of glass of which the mirror forms a part; lies outside the mirror (in front of concave, behind convex).
  • 🔹 Radius of Curvature (R): The linear distance between Pole P and Centre of Curvature C (PC = R).
  • 🔹 Principal Axis: The straight imaginary reference line passing through the Pole (P) and Centre of Curvature (C), perpendicular to the mirror surface.
  • 🔹 Aperture: The effective circular diameter of the light-reflecting surface.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 135–136):

"Fig. 9.2 — Geometric parameters of spherical mirrors: (a) Concave mirror, (b) Convex mirror."

🖼️ Fig. 9.2 – Geometric Anatomy & Parameters of Spherical Mirrors

📖 Source: NCERT Page 135–136

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.2 • Geometric Anatomy & Parameters of Spherical Mirrors

Q1: Does the Centre of Curvature (C) lie on the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror?

✅ Answer No. The centre of curvature does not lie on the mirror surface; it lies in front of a concave mirror and behind a convex mirror.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - ('No' 0.5M + location relative to mirror 0.5M)

Q2: Define the term 'aperture' of a spherical mirror.

✅ Answer The aperture is the effective diameter of the circular outline of the spherical mirror's reflecting surface.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (mentions diameter of reflecting surface)

Q3: What is the geometric angle between the Principal Axis and the mirror surface at the Pole?

✅ Answer The principal axis is exactly perpendicular (at 90°) to the mirror surface at its Pole.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (perpendicular / normal at pole)

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.2 • Concentrating Sunlight with a Concave Mirror (NCERT Page 136)

⚠️ CAUTION: Do not look directly at the Sun or its reflection with naked eyes; it may permanently damage your retinas.
  • Hold a concave mirror in your hand and direct its reflecting surface towards the Sun.
  • Direct the light reflected by the mirror onto a sheet of paper held close to the mirror.
  • Move the sheet of paper gradually back and forth until you find a bright, sharp spot of light on the paper.
  • Hold the mirror and paper in the same position for a few minutes. What do you observe? Why?
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

The paper begins to smoke and rapidly catches fire! The concave mirror converges all parallel incident solar rays to a single intense point called the Principal Focus (F). The concentrated radiant solar energy produces extreme thermal heat.

💡 Key Takeaway: The sharp spot of light is a real, point-sized image of the Sun. The distance of this spot from the mirror gives the approximate focal length (f).

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.3: Principal Focus and Focal Length of Spherical Mirrors (Page 136)

  • 🔹 Concave Mirror Focus [Fig. 9.3(a)]: Parallel incoming rays converge inwards to physically intersect at a single point F on the axis in front of the mirror, forming a Real Principal Focus.
  • 🔹 Convex Mirror Focus [Fig. 9.3(b)]: Parallel incoming rays reflect outward, appearing to diverge from a single point F situated behind the mirror, forming a Virtual Principal Focus.
  • 🔹 Radius vs. Focal Length Relation: For spherical mirrors of small aperture, the focal length is exactly half the radius of curvature: f = R / 2.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 136):

"Fig. 9.3 — Focus and focal length: (a) Concave mirror converges parallel rays to real focus F; (b) Convex mirror diverges parallel rays from virtual focus F."

🖼️ Fig. 9.3 – Principal Focus and Focal Length of Spherical Mirrors

📖 Source: NCERT Page 136

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.3 • Principal Focus and Focal Length of Spherical Mirrors

Q1: Why is a concave mirror called a converging mirror, while a convex mirror is called a diverging mirror?

✅ Answer A concave mirror reflects parallel rays inwards to intersect at a focus point (converging). A convex mirror reflects parallel rays outwards away from each other (diverging).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (0.5M concave converging + 0.5M convex diverging)

Q2: What is the nature of the principal focus of a concave mirror compared to that of a convex mirror?

✅ Answer The focus of a concave mirror is real (rays physically intersect). The focus of a convex mirror is virtual (rays only appear to diverge from behind).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (real for concave + virtual for convex)

Q3: If the radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is 28 cm, what is its focal length?

✅ Answer Using formula f = R / 2 = 28 / 2 = 14 cm. The focal length is 14 cm.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (formula 0.5M + calculation 0.5M)

🧠 Memory Hook — Radius vs. Focal Length:

"Center is double, Focus is half — R = 2f makes you pass!"
Remember that the principal focus F lies exactly at the midpoint between the Pole P and the Centre of Curvature C.

⚖️

Quick Comparison: Concave Mirror vs. Convex Mirror

Parameter Concave Mirror (Converging) Convex Mirror (Diverging)
Reflecting Surface Curved inwards (toward centre of sphere) Curved outwards (bulges towards viewer)
Action on Parallel Rays Converges parallel rays to a single real focus Diverges rays outward from a virtual focus
Nature of Focus (F) Real focus (in front of mirror, rays physically meet) Virtual focus (behind mirror, rays appear to diverge)
Focal Length Sign (Cartesian) Negative (−): measured to the left of Pole Positive (+): measured to the right of Pole
Image Types Produced Both real & inverted (5 positions) and virtual & erect (1 position) Only virtual, erect, and diminished images
🔑 Key Technical Terms & Definitions • Section 1 ▼
Reflection of Light Spherical Mirror Concave Mirror Convex Mirror Pole (P) Centre of Curvature (C) Radius of Curvature (R) Principal Axis Principal Focus (F) Focal Length (f) Aperture
  • Reflection of Light: The bouncing back of light rays into the same medium when striking an interface or polished surface.
  • Spherical Mirror: A curved mirror whose reflecting surface forms part of a hollow sphere of glass.
  • Concave Mirror: A spherical mirror curved inward toward the centre of the sphere (converging reflector).
  • Convex Mirror: A spherical mirror curved outward away from the centre of the sphere (diverging reflector).
  • Pole (P): The geometric midpoint of the light-reflecting surface of a spherical mirror.
  • Centre of Curvature (C): The centre of the hollow sphere of glass of which the spherical mirror forms a section.
  • Radius of Curvature (R): The linear distance between Pole P and Centre of Curvature C (PC = R).
  • Principal Axis: The imaginary straight reference line passing through the Pole (P) and Centre of Curvature (C).
  • Principal Focus (F): The point on the axis where rays parallel to the axis either converge (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex).
  • Focal Length (f): The linear distance between the Pole (P) and the Principal Focus (F) of a spherical mirror.
  • Aperture: The effective diameter of the circular outline of a spherical mirror's reflecting surface.

Topic 1 Quick Concept Check

❓ Q1 (MCQ): A spherical mirror has a radius of curvature of 30 cm. Its focal length is:
(a) 30 cm   (b) 60 cm   (c) 15 cm   (d) 10 cm
✅ Answer (c) 15 cm
Explanation: The focal length of a spherical mirror of small aperture is half of its radius of curvature: f = R / 2 = 30 / 2 = 15 cm.
❓ Q2 (True/False): The centre of curvature of a spherical mirror always lies on its reflecting surface.
✅ Answer False.
Explanation: The centre of curvature C lies outside the mirror surface (in front of concave, behind convex). It is the Pole (P) that lies on the reflecting surface.
❓ Q3 (Fill in the blank): When light falls normally on a plane mirror, the angle of incidence is _______ and angle of reflection is _______.
✅ Answer 0° and 0°.
Explanation: Normal incidence means the ray coincides with the normal. Hence, angle of incidence is 0°. By the first law, ∠r = ∠i = 0°, so the ray retraces its path backwards.

9.4 Exploring Image Formation by Concave Mirrors (Page 137)

How do spherical mirrors form images? What determines the nature, size, and position of the image? In Activity 9.3, we systematically vary the object's distance from a concave mirror to observe image transformations across space.

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.3 • Observing Images Formed by a Concave Mirror (NCERT Page 137)

  • Determine the approximate focal length of a concave mirror by focusing distant trees on a paper screen (per Activity 9.2).
  • Mark a straight line on a long table. Mark points P (pole), F (focus), and C (centre of curvature) such that PF = FC = f.
  • Place a burning candle as the object far away (at infinity), then beyond C, at C, between C and F, at F, and finally between P and F.
  • In each case, move a cardboard screen back and forth until a sharp, crisp candle flame image is captured on it. Note its position, size, and whether it is upright or upside down.
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

A real, inverted image can be captured on the screen for all object positions outside the focus (at infinity, beyond C, at C, and between C and F). When the candle is moved closer than the focus (between P and F), no image can be captured on the screen; looking inside the mirror reveals a dramatically magnified, virtual, and erect image behind the mirror.

💡 Key Takeaway: Only real images can be caught on a screen because light rays physically converge there. Virtual images cannot be cast on a screen because rays only appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror.

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.4 • Drawing Ray Diagrams for Concave Mirror (NCERT Page 137)

  • Draw neat ray diagrams on paper for each of the six object positions in Table 9.1.
  • Take two convenient rays emanating from a point on the object: choose any two from (i) parallel to principal axis, (ii) passing through focus, (iii) passing through centre of curvature C, or (iv) incident obliquely at pole P.
  • Find the intersection point of the two reflected rays to locate the image.
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

The ray diagrams geometrically confirm every single observation made experimentally in Activity 9.3! The intersection of reflected rays marks the position of the real image; extrapolation backwards behind the mirror marks the virtual image.

💡 Key Takeaway: At least two rays whose paths are known after reflection are needed to locate the image point geometrically.

📐

9.5 Fundamental Rules for Ray Tracing (Pages 138–139)

To construct the image of an object by ray tracing, we draw rays originating from a point on the object. The point where at least two reflected rays intersect (or appear to intersect) gives the position of the image. For convenience, we choose any two of the canonical rays:

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.4: Ray Tracing Rule 1: Ray Parallel to Principal Axis (Page 138)

  • 🔹 Concave Mirror Behavior [Fig. 9.4(a)]: A ray parallel to the principal axis passes directly through the principal focus (F) on the principal axis after reflection.
  • 🔹 Convex Mirror Behavior [Fig. 9.4(b)]: A ray parallel to the principal axis reflects outward such that it appears to diverge from the principal focus (F) situated behind the mirror.
  • 🔹 Normal to Mirror Surface: The straight line joining the centre of curvature (C) to the point of incidence acts as the normal (radius vector) to the spherical mirror surface at that point.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 138):

"Fig. 9.4 — (a) Concave mirror and (b) convex mirror: Path of a ray incident parallel to the principal axis."

🖼️ Fig. 9.4 – Ray Tracing Rule 1: Ray Parallel to Principal Axis

📖 Source: NCERT Page 138

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.4 • Ray Tracing Rule 1: Ray Parallel to Principal Axis

Q1: Where does a ray parallel to the principal axis go after reflecting from a concave mirror?

✅ Answer After reflection from a concave mirror, it passes directly through the principal focus (F) on the principal axis.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (explicit mention of principal focus F)

Q2: How does the reflected ray behave in a convex mirror when the incident ray is parallel to the principal axis?

✅ Answer It reflects outwards in such a direction that it appears to diverge from the principal focus (F) situated behind the mirror.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (appears to diverge from virtual focus F)

Q3: Why is the line joining the Centre of Curvature C to the point of incidence considered the normal?

✅ Answer Because a radius of a sphere is always perpendicular to the tangent at any point on the spherical surface. Hence, line segment CP is the normal to the mirror at the point of incidence.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (radius is perpendicular to tangent on spherical surface)

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.5: Ray Tracing Rule 2: Ray Passing Through Focus (Page 139)

  • 🔹 Concave Mirror Focus Ray [Fig. 9.5(a)]: A ray of light passing through the principal focus (F) strikes the mirror and emerges parallel to the principal axis after reflection.
  • 🔹 Convex Mirror Focus Ray [Fig. 9.5(b)]: A ray directed towards the principal focus (F) behind a convex mirror reflects and emerges parallel to the principal axis.
  • 🔹 Principle of Reversibility: Rule 2 is the exact reverse of Rule 1; reversing the direction of light causes it to retrace its exact original trajectory.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 139):

"Fig. 9.5 — (a) Concave mirror and (b) convex mirror: Path of a ray passing through or directed towards the focus."

🖼️ Fig. 9.5 – Ray Tracing Rule 2: Ray Passing Through Focus

📖 Source: NCERT Page 139

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.5 • Ray Tracing Rule 2: Ray Passing Through Focus

Q1: What path does a ray follow after reflection if it passes through the focus of a concave mirror?

✅ Answer It reflects and emerges parallel to the principal axis.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (emerges parallel to principal axis)

Q2: State the optical principle that makes Rule 2 the exact inverse of Rule 1.

✅ Answer The Principle of Reversibility of Light, which states that light rays retrace their exact path if their direction of travel is reversed.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Principle of Reversibility of Light)

Q3: In a convex mirror, how must an incident ray be oriented to emerge parallel to the principal axis?

✅ Answer It must be directed towards the virtual principal focus (F) situated behind the mirror.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (directed towards virtual focus F)

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.6: Ray Tracing Rule 3: Ray Passing Through Centre of Curvature (Page 139)

  • 🔹 Concave Mirror Normal Ray [Fig. 9.6(a)]: A ray passing through the centre of curvature (C) strikes the mirror along the normal (∠i = 0°) and reflects back along the exact same path.
  • 🔹 Convex Mirror Normal Ray [Fig. 9.6(b)]: A ray directed towards the centre of curvature (C) behind a convex mirror reflects straight back along its line of incidence.
  • 🔹 Zero Angle of Incidence: Because the incident ray falls along the normal (radius of the sphere), ∠i = 0°, hence ∠r = 0°.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 139):

"Fig. 9.6 — (a) Concave mirror and (b) convex mirror: Path of a ray passing through or directed towards the centre of curvature."

🖼️ Fig. 9.6 – Ray Tracing Rule 3: Ray Passing Through Centre of Curvature

📖 Source: NCERT Page 139

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.6 • Ray Tracing Rule 3: Ray Passing Through Centre of Curvature

Q1: Why does a ray passing through the centre of curvature of a concave mirror retrace its path?

✅ Answer Because the line passing through C is a radius of the sphere, making it normal (perpendicular) to the mirror at the point of incidence. Thus, ∠i = 0°, so ∠r = 0° and the ray bounces straight back.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (falls normally on mirror surface / ∠i = 0°)

Q2: What is the value of the angle of incidence when a ray passes through C?

✅ Answer The angle of incidence is exactly 0° (zero degrees).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (0°)

Q3: Does this normal reflection rule hold true for convex mirrors as well?

✅ Answer Yes. Any ray directed towards the centre of curvature C behind a convex mirror strikes normally and reflects straight back along its incident path.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Yes, applies to convex mirrors directed towards C)

🎯

Ray Tracing Rule 4 • Oblique Ray Incident at the Pole (Page 139)

A ray of light incident obliquely to the principal axis towards the Pole (P) of a concave mirror or convex mirror reflects obliquely such that:

∠i = ∠r

The incident ray and reflected ray follow the laws of reflection strictly at the Pole, making equal angles with the principal axis.

Position of Object Position of Image Size of Image Nature of Image

Beyond C Between F and C Diminished Real and inverted

Between C and F Beyond C Enlarged (magnified) Real and inverted
At F At infinity Image would not be formed
➕ NCERT 2026–27 Verbatim Update

💡 Pedagogical Clarification on Row 5 ("At F"): The NCERT 2026–27 edition prints "Image would not be formed" because reflected rays become parallel and never intersect at any finite distance on a laboratory screen. In classical ray optics, parallel rays are considered to meet at infinity, forming a highly enlarged, real and inverted image. Both representations are physically sound.

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.7: Ray Diagrams for Concave Mirror (6 Canonical Positions) (Page 140)

  • 🔹 Object at Infinity [Fig. 9.7(a)]: Parallel rays converge at focus F; image is real, inverted, and extremely diminished (point-sized).
  • 🔹 Object Beyond C [Fig. 9.7(b)]: Reflected rays intersect between C and F; image is real, inverted, and diminished.
  • 🔹 Object at C [Fig. 9.7(c)]: Reflected rays intersect at C; image is real, inverted, and of the exact same size as the object.
  • 🔹 Object Between C and F [Fig. 9.7(d)]: Reflected rays intersect beyond C; image is real, inverted, and magnified (enlarged).
  • 🔹 Object at F [Fig. 9.7(e)]: Reflected rays emerge parallel; image is formed at infinity, highly magnified (NCERT 2026–27: 'Image would not be formed' on screen).
  • 🔹 Object Between P and F [Fig. 9.7(f)]: Reflected rays diverge; backward extensions intersect behind mirror, forming a virtual, erect, and magnified image.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 140):

"Fig. 9.7 — Ray diagrams for the formation of image by a concave mirror for various positions of the object: (a) at infinity, (b) beyond C, (c) at C, (d) between C and F, (e) at F, and (f) between P and F."

🖼️ Fig. 9.7 – Ray Diagrams for Concave Mirror (6 Canonical Positions)

📖 Source: NCERT Page 140

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.7 • Ray Diagrams for Concave Mirror (6 Canonical Positions)

Q1: In which specific position does a concave mirror form a virtual, erect, and magnified image?

✅ Answer When the object is placed between the Pole (P) and the Principal Focus (F) [Figure 9.7(f)].

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Between P and F)

Q2: Where must an object be placed in front of a concave mirror so that its image is formed at the same position and of the same size?

✅ Answer The object must be placed exactly at the Centre of Curvature (C) [Figure 9.7(c)].

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (At Centre of Curvature C)

Q3: Why can the image formed in case (f) not be obtained on a screen?

✅ Answer Because the image is virtual. The reflected rays do not actually intersect in front of the mirror; they only appear to meet when extended backwards behind the mirror.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Image is virtual / reflected rays only appear to intersect behind mirror)

9.6 Real-World Applications & Uses of Concave Mirrors (Page 140)

1. Torches, Searchlights & Vehicle Headlights:

The light source (filament) is placed precisely at the Principal Focus (F) of the concave reflector. The reflected light emerges as a powerful, parallel beam that travels long distances without spreading out.

2. Shaving & Makeup Mirrors:

When the face is placed close to the mirror (between Pole P and Focus F), the mirror forms an erect and enlarged (magnified) virtual image, facilitating precise shaving and grooming.

3. Dentists' Examination Mirrors:

Dentists hold small concave mirrors inside the patient's mouth close to teeth to see an enlarged, erect view of hidden dental cavities.

4. Solar Furnaces & Cookers:

Large concave reflectors converge incoming parallel solar rays onto a small focal zone, generating extreme temperatures exceeding 3000°C without electricity!

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.5 • Observing Images in a Convex Mirror (NCERT Page 141)

  • Take a convex mirror. Hold a pencil in an upright position in front of it.
  • Observe the image of the pencil in the mirror. Is it erect or inverted? Diminished or enlarged?
  • Move the pencil slowly away from the mirror. Does the image become smaller or larger?
  • State whether the image moves closer to or farther away from the focus as the pencil moves away.
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

The image is always erect, virtual, and diminished (smaller than object). As the pencil moves farther away, the image moves closer to the focus F behind the mirror and gets progressively smaller, approaching a point size at infinity.

💡 Key Takeaway: A convex mirror never forms an inverted or magnified image of a real object!

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.6 • Field of View & Full-Length Images (Agra Fort Observation) (NCERT Page 141)

  • Observe the image of a distant, tall object (such as a tall tree or multistory building) in a small plane mirror. Can you see a full-length image?
  • Try with plane mirrors of different sizes. Did you succeed in seeing the entire object?
  • Repeat the activity with a concave mirror. Can you see the full object?
  • Now try with a convex mirror. Did you see the full-length image of the distant object?
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

You can see a full-length image of a tall, distant object only in a convex mirror because of its wide, curved-outward field of view! A small plane mirror or concave mirror cannot capture the full field of a tall monument.

💡 Key Takeaway: One such large convex mirror is historically fitted on the wall of Agra Fort facing the Taj Mahal. An observer standing at the tomb can see the full view of the Taj Mahal in it!

9.7 Image Formation & Applications of Convex Mirrors (Pages 141–142)

📖 Table 9.2 Verbatim Reference: NCERT Class 10 Science (Page 142).

Position of Object Position of Image Size of Image Nature of Image
At infinity At the focus F, behind the mirror Highly diminished, point-sized Virtual and erect
Between infinity and pole P Between P and F, behind the mirror Diminished Virtual and erect
🚗 Real-World Uses of Convex Mirrors:

Convex mirrors are universally employed as rear-view (wing) mirrors in automobiles because they always form an erect, diminished image and give a wider field of view curving outwards. They are also installed at sharp hallway turns in hospitals, large superstores (anti-theft), and blind hairpin bends.

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.8: Formation of Image by a Convex Mirror (Page 141)

  • 🔹 Object at Infinity [Fig. 9.8(a)]: Incident parallel rays reflect outward; backward dashed lines meet at focus F behind the mirror, forming a virtual, erect, and highly diminished (point-sized) image.
  • 🔹 Object Between Infinity and Pole P [Fig. 9.8(b)]: Ray 1 parallel to the axis appears to diverge from F; Ray 2 directed towards C reflects straight back. The rays intersect between P and F behind the mirror, forming a virtual, erect, and diminished image.
  • 🔹 Curved Outward Geometry: Because a convex mirror curves outward, it provides a much wider angular field than a flat plane mirror, enabling drivers to see large traffic zones behind them.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 141):

"Fig. 9.8 — Formation of image by a convex mirror: (a) at infinity, and (b) at a finite distance between infinity and pole P."

🖼️ Fig. 9.8 – Formation of Image by a Convex Mirror

📖 Source: NCERT Page 141

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.8 • Formation of Image by a Convex Mirror

Q1: State the two essential characteristics of any image formed by a convex mirror.

✅ Answer Images formed by a convex mirror are always virtual, erect, and diminished (smaller than the object).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Virtual & erect 0.5M + diminished 0.5M)

Q2: Where is the image located when an object is at infinity in front of a convex mirror?

✅ Answer The image is formed at the principal focus (F) behind the mirror.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (At focus F behind the mirror)

Q3: Why does a convex mirror offer a much wider field of view than a plane mirror of the same size?

✅ Answer Because a convex mirror is curved outwards, allowing it to capture light rays from a substantially broader angular perimeter compared to a flat plane mirror.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Curved outwards capturing broader angular perimeter)

❓

9.8 In-Text Questions • NCERT Page 142 (Complete Verbatim Solutions)

📌 In-Text Question 1 (Page 142)

Define the principal focus of a concave mirror.

✅ Answer

The principal focus of a concave mirror is a specific point on its principal axis where all incident light rays that travel parallel and close to the principal axis converge and intersect after reflecting from the mirror.

It is denoted by the letter F and is a real focus situated in front of the reflecting surface.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Point on principal axis where parallel rays converge after reflection)
📌 In-Text Question 2 (Page 142)

The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is 20 cm. What is its focal length?

✅ Answer

Given: Radius of curvature R = 20 cm.

Formula: f = R / 2

Calculation: f = 20 / 2 = 10 cm.

Answer: The focal length of the spherical mirror is 10 cm.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Formula f = R/2 0.5M + Calculation f = 10 cm 0.5M)
📌 In-Text Question 3 (Page 142)

Name a mirror that can give an erect and enlarged image of an object.

✅ Answer

A concave mirror can give an erect and enlarged (magnified) image of an object, when the object is placed very close to the mirror — specifically between its Pole (P) and Principal Focus (F).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Concave mirror 0.5M + Condition between P and F 0.5M)
📌 In-Text Question 4 (Page 142)

Why do we prefer a convex mirror as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?

✅ Answer

We prefer a convex mirror as a rear-view (wing) mirror in automobiles due to two decisive reasons:

  1. Always Erect Image: It always produces an erect (upright), though diminished, image of trailing vehicles, preventing confusion while driving.
  2. Wider Field of View: Because a convex mirror is curved outwards, it captures light across a vastly wider angular field than a flat plane mirror, enabling the driver to monitor much larger traffic areas behind them safely.
📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks - (1M always erect/diminished + 1M curved outwards giving wider field of view)
🔑 Key Technical Terms & Definitions • Section 2 ▼
Real Image Virtual Image Converging Mirror Diverging Mirror Field of View Dentist's Mirror Searchlight Mirror
  • Real Image: An image formed when reflected or refracted light rays physically meet and intersect; it can be captured on a screen and is always inverted.
  • Virtual Image: An image formed when reflected or refracted rays only appear to diverge from a point; it cannot be captured on a screen and is always erect.
  • Converging Mirror: Another name for a concave mirror, because it gathers parallel incoming rays toward a common focus point.
  • Diverging Mirror: Another name for a convex mirror, because it spreads parallel incoming rays outward away from each other.
  • Field of View: The entire observable angular area that a driver or optical device can see through a mirror or lens at any given moment.
  • Dentist's Mirror: A concave mirror used by dental surgeons to produce an enlarged, erect virtual view of patients' teeth.
  • Searchlight Mirror: A concave reflector with the bulb placed exactly at its focus F to produce an intense, parallel beam of light.
📝

Topic 2 Quick Concept Check

❓ Q1 (MCQ): A burning candle is placed 20 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. The image formed will be:
(a) at 20 cm, real   (b) at infinity   (c) between F and C   (d) behind mirror
✅ Answer (b) at infinity
Explanation: When the object is placed at the principal focus (u = -f = -20 cm), the reflected rays emerge parallel and meet at infinity.
❓ Q2 (True/False): A convex mirror can form a real inverted image if the object is placed between the pole and focus.
✅ Answer False.
Explanation: A convex mirror never forms a real image of a real object under any circumstances! All images formed by a convex mirror are strictly virtual, erect, and diminished.
❓ Q3 (Fill in the blank): To produce a parallel beam of light in car headlights, the light bulb is placed at the _______ of the concave reflector.
✅ Answer Principal Focus (F).
Explanation: By the principle of reversibility (Rule 2), light rays originating from the focus reflect parallel to the principal axis, creating a concentrated long-range beam.
🎯 3. Sign Convention, Mirror Formula & Magnification (Pages 143–145)
➕

9.9 New Cartesian Sign Convention (Pages 143–144)

To eliminate ambiguity when solving ray optics problems, we employ a geometric coordinate convention termed the New Cartesian Sign Convention. The Pole (P) of the mirror is placed at the origin (0, 0), and the principal axis serves as the X-axis (X'X).

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.9: The New Cartesian Sign Convention for Spherical Mirrors (Page 143)

  • 🔹 Pole (P) as Origin: The Pole (P) of the spherical mirror is taken as the origin (0, 0); the principal axis is taken as the coordinate X-axis (X'X).
  • 🔹 Incident Light Direction: The object is always placed to the left of the mirror; incident light travels from left to right.
  • 🔹 Distances Along X-Axis: Distances measured in the direction of incident light (to the right of Pole) are positive (+); distances measured against incident light (to the left of Pole) are negative (−).
  • 🔹 Heights Along Y-Axis: Heights measured upward and perpendicular to the principal axis are positive (+); heights measured downward below the axis are negative (−).

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 143):

"Fig. 9.9 — The New Cartesian Sign Convention for mirrors."

🖼️ Fig. 9.9 – The New Cartesian Sign Convention for Spherical Mirrors

📖 Source: NCERT Page 143

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.9 • The New Cartesian Sign Convention for Spherical Mirrors

Q1: What point on the spherical mirror is chosen as the origin for coordinate measurements?

✅ Answer The Pole (P) of the spherical mirror is chosen as the origin (0, 0).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Pole P as origin)

Q2: What is the Cartesian sign of object distance (u) for real objects in spherical mirrors?

✅ Answer The object distance u is always negative (−) because the object is always placed to the left of the mirror.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Always negative / -)

Q3: What are the signs of focal lengths for a concave mirror and a convex mirror respectively?

✅ Answer The focal length f of a concave mirror is negative (−), whereas that of a convex mirror is positive (+).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (0.5M concave negative + 0.5M convex positive)

🧠 Memory Hook — Cartesian Sign Rules:

"Left is Loss (−), Right is Right (+);
Up is Upright (+), Down is Depressed (−)!"

📐

9.10 The Mirror Formula & Linear Magnification (Pages 144–145)

In a spherical mirror, the distance of the object from its pole is called the object distance (u). The distance of the image from the pole of the mirror is called the image distance (v). The distance of the principal focus from the pole is called the focal length (f).

🌟 The Mirror Formula:

1/v + 1/u = 1/f

This formula is universally valid in all situations for all spherical mirrors (both concave and convex) for all positions of the object. Always substitute values with their proper Cartesian signs!

🌟 Linear Magnification (m):

Magnification produced by a spherical mirror gives the relative extent to which the image of an object is magnified with respect to the object size:

m = Height of Image (h') / Height of Object (h) = - v / u
🔍 Physical Meaning of Sign and Magnitude of 'm':
  • Negative sign of m (m < 0): The image is real and inverted (since h' is negative below axis).
  • Positive sign of m (m > 0): The image is virtual and erect (since h' is positive above axis).
  • |m| > 1: Image is enlarged (magnified).
  • |m| = 1: Image is same size as object.
  • |m| < 1: Image is diminished (smaller).

📐 NCERT Solved Example 9.1 (Page 144) (Page 144)

A convex mirror used for rear-view on an automobile has a radius of curvature of 3.00 m. If a bus is located at 5.00 m from this mirror, find the position, nature and size of the image.
📝 Step-by-Step Solution:
1. Given Quantities with Cartesian Signs:
Radius of curvature, R = +3.00 m
Object distance, u = -5.00 m
Image distance, v = ?
Height / Magnification, m = ?
2. Calculate Focal Length (f):
f = R / 2 = +3.00 / 2 = +1.50 m (Convex mirror has a positive focal length)
3. Apply the Mirror Formula:
1/v + 1/u = 1/f  ⇒  1/v = 1/f - 1/u
4. Substitute Numerical Values:
1/v = 1/(+1.50) - 1/(-5.00) = 1/1.50 + 1/5.00
1/v = 5.00 / 7.50 + 1.50 / 7.50 = 6.50 / 7.50
v = +7.50 / 6.50 = +1.15 m
5. Calculate Magnification (m):
m = -v / u = -(+1.15) / (-5.00) = +0.23
🎯 Final Result: Image is formed at +1.15 m behind the mirror. It is virtual, erect, and diminished to 0.23 times the size of the bus.
✅ Verification: For convex mirror, image must always fall between Pole and Focus (0 < v < +1.50 m), and m must be positive and less than 1. Here v = +1.15 m and m = +0.23 — perfectly verified! ✓

📐 NCERT Solved Example 9.2 (Page 145) (Page 145)

An object, 4.0 cm in size, is placed at 25.0 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15.0 cm. At what distance from the mirror should a screen be placed in order to obtain a sharp image? Find the nature and the size of the image.
📝 Step-by-Step Solution:
1. Given Quantities with Cartesian Signs:
Size of object, h = +4.0 cm
Object distance, u = -25.0 cm
Focal length, f = -15.0 cm (Concave mirror has negative focal length)
Image distance, v = ?
Image height, h' = ?
2. Apply Mirror Formula:
1/v + 1/u = 1/f  ⇒  1/v = 1/f - 1/u
3. Substitute Numerical Values:
1/v = 1/(-15.0) - 1/(-25.0) = -1/15.0 + 1/25.0
Take LCM of 15 and 25 (= 75):
1/v = (-5 + 3) / 75 = -2 / 75
v = -75 / 2 = -37.5 cm
4. Calculate Image Height (h'):
m = h' / h = -v / u  ⇒  h' = - (v / u) × h
h' = - [ (-37.5) / (-25.0) ] × (+4.0)
h' = - (1.5) × 4.0 = -6.0 cm
5. Magnification Value:
m = h' / h = -6.0 / +4.0 = -1.5
🎯 Final Result: The screen should be placed at 37.5 cm in front of the mirror (v = -37.5 cm). The image is real, inverted, and enlarged (6.0 cm tall).
✅ Verification: Object lies between C (30 cm) and F (15 cm). For this position, ray optics predicts image beyond C (v > 30 cm) and enlarged. Our v = -37.5 cm and h' = -6.0 cm match theory exactly! ✓
❓

📌 In-Text Question 1 (Page 145)

Find the focal length of a convex mirror whose radius of curvature is 32 cm.

✅ Answer

Given: Radius of curvature of convex mirror, R = +32 cm.

Formula: f = R / 2

Calculation: f = +32 / 2 = +16 cm.

Answer: The focal length of the convex mirror is +16 cm.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Formula f = R/2 0.5M + Answer +16 cm 0.5M)
📌 In-Text Question 2 (Page 145)

A concave mirror produces three times magnified (enlarged) real image of an object placed at 10 cm in front of it. Where is the image located?

✅ Answer

Given:

  • Object distance, u = -10 cm
  • Magnification, m = -3 (Negative because the image is real and inverted)

Formula: m = -v / u

Calculation:
-3 = -v / (-10)
-3 = v / 10  ⇒  v = -3 × 10 = -30 cm

Answer: The image is located at a distance of 30 cm in front of the concave mirror (on the same side as the object).

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks - (1M sign of m = -3 and formula m = -v/u + 1M calculation v = -30 cm)
🔑 Key Technical Terms & Definitions • Section 3 ▼
Cartesian Sign Convention Object Distance (u) Image Distance (v) Mirror Formula Magnification (m)
  • Cartesian Sign Convention: The standard sign rules used in optics where the pole/optical centre serves as the origin, right is positive, left is negative, up is positive, and down is negative.
  • Object Distance (u): The distance measured from the pole of the mirror to the location of the object; always negative for real objects.
  • Image Distance (v): The distance measured from the pole of the mirror to the location of the image; negative for real images in front, positive for virtual images behind.
  • Mirror Formula: The universal algebraic equation connecting object distance u, image distance v, and focal length f: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f.
  • Magnification (m): The ratio of the height of the image (h') to the height of the object (h), equal to -v/u for spherical mirrors.
📝

Topic 3 Quick Concept Check

❓ Q1 (MCQ): The magnification produced by a plane mirror is always:
(a) 0   (b) -1   (c) +1   (d) between 0 and 1
✅ Answer (c) +1
Explanation: The plus sign indicates that the image is virtual and erect. The value 1 indicates that the size of the image is exactly equal to the size of the object (h' = h).
❓ Q2 (True/False): The mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f can be used without sign conventions as long as distances are positive.
✅ Answer False.
Explanation: The mirror formula is valid only when proper Cartesian signs are assigned to every known quantity (u, v, f). Omitting signs will lead to mathematically incorrect results.
❓ Q3 (Calculation): If a concave mirror forms a real image of size 6 cm for an object of size 2 cm, the magnification is:
✅ Answer m = -3.
Explanation: For a real image, the image is inverted, so h' = -6 cm. Object height h = +2 cm. Magnification m = h' / h = -6 / 2 = -3.
🎯 4. Refraction of Light & Optical Density (Pages 146–150)
🌊

9.12 Everyday Refraction Phenomena & Laboratory Activities (Pages 146–147)

Light seems to travel along straight-line paths in a single uniform transparent medium. But what happens when light enters from one transparent medium to another? Does it still follow a straight line, or does it change its direction?

We recall common day-to-day observations:

  • The bottom of a tank, bucket, or swimming pool filled with water appears to be raised.
  • A straight pencil partly immersed in water in a glass tumbler appears to be bent and displaced at the water-air interface.
  • Letters of printed matter appear raised when a thick glass paperweight is placed over them.
  • A fresh lemon kept in water in a glass tumbler appears larger than its actual size when viewed from the sides.
💡 Scientific Cause of Refraction: Refraction occurs because light travels with different speeds in different transparent media! Light travels fastest in vacuum/air (3 × 108 m s-1), but slows down significantly in denser media like water (2.25 × 108 m s-1), glass (2.00 × 108 m s-1), and diamond (1.24 × 108 m s-1).

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.7 • Apparent Depth of Coin in Water Bucket (NCERT Page 146)

  • Place a coin at the bottom of a bucket filled with water.
  • With your eye to a side above water, try to pick up the coin in one go. Did you succeed?
  • Repeat with friends. Why is it difficult to grab the coin on your first attempt?
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

You miss the coin because it appears to be at a shallower depth (apparent depth) than its actual physical location! Light rays emerging obliquely from the coin into air bend away from the normal, making the coin appear raised.

💡 Key Takeaway: The bottom of a water tank or swimming pool appears shallower due to refraction.

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.8 • Reappearing Coin in a Shallow Bowl (NCERT Page 146)

  • Place a coin at the bottom of a shallow, opaque bowl on a table.
  • Move away slowly until the coin just disappears behind the rim of the bowl. Stop and do not move your eyes.
  • Ask a friend to pour water gently into the bowl without disturbing the coin. What happens?
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

The coin magically reappears into view as water is poured! As light travels obliquely from water into air at the surface, it bends away from the normal, bending over the edge of the bowl into your eyes.

💡 Key Takeaway: Refraction bends light around the opaque barrier rim, making the submerged object visible.

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.9 • Viewing a Line Through a Thick Glass Slab (NCERT Page 146)

  • Draw a thick straight line with ink on a sheet of white paper placed on a table.
  • Place a thick rectangular glass slab over the line such that one of its edges makes an angle with the line.
  • Look at the portion of the line under the slab from the sides. Does it appear bent at the edges?
  • Next, place the glass slab such that it is normal to the line. What do you observe now?
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

When viewed obliquely, the line appears bent and shifted sideward at the glass-air interfaces. When viewed normally (at 90° to the interface), the line does not bend at all; it only appears slightly raised.

💡 Key Takeaway: Refraction (bending) occurs only when light enters an interface obliquely; normal incidence produces zero deviation.

📐

9.13 Refraction Through a Rectangular Glass Slab (Pages 147–148)

To investigate the exact geometry of light refraction at parallel plane interfaces, Activity 9.10 traces the path of light through a rectangular glass slab:

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.10 • Refraction Through a Rectangular Glass Slab (NCERT Page 147)

  • Fix a sheet of white paper on a drawing board using board pins.
  • Place a rectangular glass slab in the middle. Draw its boundary ABCD with a sharp pencil.
  • Draw an incident ray EO inclined at an angle ∠i to normal NN' at surface AB. Fix two pins E and F vertically on this line.
  • Look through the glass slab from the opposite face CD. Fix two more pins G and H such that the feet of all four pins lie in a straight line.
  • Remove the slab and pins. Join G and H to meet CD at O'. Join O and O'. Draw normal MM' at face CD.
  • Measure angle of incidence ∠i, angle of refraction ∠r, and emergent angle ∠e.
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

Key Measurements & Inferences:

  • At interface AB (Air → Glass): Light enters from rarer to denser medium and bends towards the normal (∠r < ∠i).
  • At interface CD (Glass → Air): Light enters from denser to rarer medium and bends away from the normal (∠e > ∠r').
  • Since the opposite refracting faces AB and CD are strictly parallel, the extent of bending at both interfaces is equal and opposite. Hence, the emergent ray is exactly parallel to the incident ray (∠i = ∠e).
  • The emergent ray is shifted sideward by a perpendicular distance called Lateral Displacement.

💡 Key Takeaway: Lateral displacement is directly proportional to slab thickness, refractive index of glass, and angle of incidence.

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.10: Refraction of Light Through a Rectangular Glass Slab (Page 148)

  • 🔹 Incident Ray (EO): Travelling through air, strikes surface AB at point of incidence O at an angle of incidence ∠i.
  • 🔹 Refracted Ray (OO'): Inside the optically denser glass slab, bends towards the normal NN' at an angle of refraction ∠r (where ∠r < ∠i).
  • 🔹 Emergent Ray (O'H): Emerging from glass into rarer air at surface CD, bends away from normal MM' at emergent angle ∠e.
  • 🔹 Lateral Displacement (d): Because surfaces AB and CD are strictly parallel planes, ∠i = ∠e; the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted laterally by distance d.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 148):

"Fig. 9.10 — Refraction of light through a rectangular glass slab."

🖼️ Fig. 9.10 – Refraction of Light Through a Rectangular Glass Slab

📖 Source: NCERT Page 148

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.10 • Refraction of Light Through a Rectangular Glass Slab

Q1: Why does the emergent ray from a rectangular glass slab travel parallel to the incident ray?

✅ Answer Because the refracting surfaces AB and CD are parallel planes, making the bending of light at interface AB (towards normal) equal and opposite to the bending at interface CD (away from normal). Thus, ∠i = ∠e.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Opposite faces are parallel → equal and opposite bending)

Q2: What is meant by 'lateral displacement' in glass slab refraction?

✅ Answer Lateral displacement is the perpendicular distance separating the emergent ray from the original uninterrupted straight-line path of the incident ray.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Perpendicular distance between original path and emergent ray)

Q3: What happens to a ray of light that strikes the glass slab interface normally (∠i = 0°)?

✅ Answer A ray incident normally (∠i = 0°) passes straight through without any deviation or lateral displacement (∠r = 0°).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Passes undeviated / no bending)

📜

9.14 The Laws of Refraction & Snell's Law (Pages 148–149)

Careful experimental observations of refraction through transparent media lead to two universal laws of refraction:

📜 The Two Universal Laws of Refraction:

  1. First Law: The incident ray, the refracted ray, and the normal to the interface of two transparent media at the point of incidence, all lie in the same plane.
  2. Second Law (Snell's Law of Refraction): The ratio of sine of angle of incidence to the sine of angle of refraction is a constant, for the light of a given colour and for the given pair of media:
    sin i / sin r = constant = n21
    This constant value is called the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first.
📊

9.15 Relative vs. Absolute Refractive Index & Material Media (Pages 148–150)

The extent of the change in direction that takes place in a given pair of media may be expressed in terms of the refractive index. It is fundamentally linked to the relative speed of propagation of light in different media.

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.11: Refraction of Light at Boundary of Two Media (Page 148)

  • 🔹 Medium 1 to Medium 2 Transition: A light ray leaves Medium 1 (speed v1) and enters Medium 2 (speed v2) across a flat boundary interface.
  • 🔹 Relative Refractive Index (n21): Defined as the ratio of speed of light in Medium 1 to speed in Medium 2: n21 = v1 / v2.
  • 🔹 Reciprocity Principle: Refractive index of Medium 1 with respect to Medium 2 is the exact reciprocal: n12 = 1 / n21 = v2 / v1.
  • 🔹 Unitless Physical Quantity: Because refractive index is a ratio of two identical dimensions (speeds), it is completely unitless and dimensionless.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 148):

"Fig. 9.11 — Refraction of light."

🖼️ Fig. 9.11 – Refraction of Light at Boundary of Two Media

📖 Source: NCERT Page 148

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.11 • Refraction of Light at Boundary of Two Media

Q1: Define the refractive index of Medium 2 with respect to Medium 1 in terms of wave velocities.

✅ Answer It is defined as the ratio of the speed of light in Medium 1 (v1) to the speed of light in Medium 2 (v2): n21 = v1 / v2.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Ratio of speed in Medium 1 to speed in Medium 2)

Q2: What is the mathematical relation connecting n21 and n12?

✅ Answer They are reciprocal to each other: n12 = 1 / n21 (or n21 × n12 = 1).

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (n12 = 1 / n21)

Q3: Does refractive index have any SI unit?

✅ Answer No. Refractive index is a pure ratio of two identical physical quantities (speeds), so it is a dimensionless, unitless quantity.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Dimensionless / unitless)

💎

Material Medium Refractive Index (n)

Material Medium Refractive Index (n)

Crown glass1.52

⚠️ Crucial Distinction: Optical Density ≠ Mass Density!

An optically denser medium does not necessarily possess greater mass density (mass per unit volume). For example, kerosene floats on water because its mass density is lower than water. Yet, kerosene's refractive index (1.44) is higher than water's (1.33), meaning kerosene is optically denser than water and light travels slower in kerosene than in water!

🧠 Memory Hook — Ray Bending Direction:

"F-S-T: Fast to Slow bends Towards normal!
S-F-A: Slow to Fast bends Away from normal!"

9.16 In-Text Questions • NCERT Page 150 (Complete Verbatim Solutions)

📌 In-Text Question 1 (Page 150)

A ray of light travelling in air enters obliquely into water. Does the light ray bend towards the normal or away from the normal? Why?

✅ Answer

The light ray bends towards the normal.

Reason: Water is optically denser than air (nwater = 1.33 > nair ≈ 1.00). When light travels from an optically rarer medium (air) to an optically denser medium (water), its speed decreases (it slows down). By Snell's law, a decrease in speed causes the refracted ray to bend closer to the normal.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks - (1M 'towards normal' + 1M light slowing down in denser medium)
📌 In-Text Question 2 (Page 150)

Light enters from air to glass having refractive index 1.50. What is the speed of light in the glass? The speed of light in vacuum is 3 × 108 m s-1.

✅ Answer

Given:

  • Refractive index of glass, n = 1.50
  • Speed of light in vacuum, c = 3 × 108 m s-1

Formula: n = c / v  ⇒  v = c / n

Calculation:
v = (3 × 108) / 1.50 = 2 × 108 m s-1

Answer: The speed of light in glass is 2.00 × 108 m s-1.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks - (Formula v = c/n 1M + Answer 2 x 10^8 m/s with unit 1M)
📌 In-Text Question 3 (Page 150)

Find out, from Table 9.3, the medium having highest optical density. Also find the medium with lowest optical density.

✅ Answer

From Table 9.3 of NCERT Class 10:

  • Medium with Highest Optical Density: Diamond, with the highest refractive index of n = 2.42.
  • Medium with Lowest Optical Density: Air, with the lowest refractive index of n = 1.0003.
📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks - (1M Diamond n = 2.42 + 1M Air n = 1.0003)
📌 In-Text Question 4 (Page 150)

You are given kerosene, turpentine and water. In which of these does the light travel fastest? Use the information given in Table 9.3.

✅ Answer

From Table 9.3, the refractive indices are:

  • Water: n = 1.33
  • Kerosene: n = 1.44
  • Turpentine oil: n = 1.47

Scientific Principle: Speed of light is inversely proportional to refractive index: v = c / n. Therefore, light travels fastest in the medium with the lowest refractive index.

Answer: Light travels fastest in water (where v ≈ 2.26 × 108 m s-1).

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks - (Identification of water 1M + Justification that lowest n gives highest speed 1M)
📌 In-Text Question 5 (Page 150)

The refractive index of diamond is 2.42. What is the meaning of this statement?

✅ Answer

The statement means that the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum (or air) to the speed of light in diamond is equal to 2.42:

n = c / v = 2.42  ⇒  v = c / 2.42 ≈ 0.413 c

In other words, light travels 2.42 times slower in diamond than in vacuum (or speed of light in diamond is only 1 / 2.42 times its speed in vacuum, approximately 1.24 × 108 m s-1).

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks - (1M ratio c/v = 2.42 + 1M explanation that speed in diamond is 1/2.42 of speed in air/vacuum)

Refraction Optically Denser Medium Optically Rarer Medium Snell's Law Absolute Refractive Index Lateral Displacement
  • Refraction: The phenomenon of bending of a ray of light when it passes obliquely from one transparent optical medium to another of different optical density.
  • Optically Denser Medium: A medium in which the speed of light is comparatively slower and which possesses a higher refractive index.
  • Optically Rarer Medium: A medium in which the speed of light is comparatively faster and which possesses a lower refractive index.
  • Snell's Law: The fundamental law of refraction stating that the ratio of sine of angle of incidence to sine of angle of refraction is constant: sin i / sin r = constant = n21.
  • Absolute Refractive Index: The refractive index of a transparent medium with respect to vacuum (or air): n = c / v.
  • Lateral Displacement: The perpendicular distance separating the emergent ray from the original straight path of the incident ray after passing through a parallel-faced transparent slab.
📝

Topic 4 Quick Concept Check

❓ Q1 (MCQ): When light passes obliquely from glass into water, it:
(a) bends towards the normal   (b) bends away from normal   (c) passes without deviation   (d) turns back completely
✅ Answer (b) bends away from the normal
Explanation: Glass is optically denser (n = 1.5) than water (n = 1.33). When light goes from denser to rarer medium (slow to fast), it speeds up and bends away from the normal.
❓ Q2 (True/False): A liquid that floats on water must always be optically rarer than water.
✅ Answer False.
Explanation: Floating is governed by mass density, whereas optical refraction is governed by optical density (refractive index). Kerosene floats on water, yet its refractive index (1.44) is higher than water (1.33), making it optically denser!
❓ Q3 (Fill in the blank): The physical cause of lateral displacement in a glass slab is that the two opposing refracting surfaces are _______.
✅ Answer Parallel.
Explanation: Because opposite faces AB and CD are parallel planes, the bending at entry is exactly reversed at exit, producing zero angular deviation but a parallel lateral shift.

9.17 Spherical Lenses: Double Convex & Double Concave (Pages 150–152)

You might have seen watchmakers using a small magnifying glass to inspect miniature gears. Spectacles used for reading or correcting vision also use lenses. What are lenses? How do they bend light rays?

A spherical lens is a piece of transparent refracting material bound by two surfaces, of which one or both surfaces are spherical. This means that a lens is bound by at least one spherical surface; the other surface may be plane.

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.11 • Concentrating Sunlight with a Convex Lens (NCERT Page 151)

⚠️ CAUTION: Do not look directly at the Sun through any lens, as focused sunlight can instantly blind you.
  • Hold a convex lens in your hand. Direct it towards the Sun.
  • Focus the light from the Sun on a sheet of paper. Obtain a sharp, bright spot on the paper.
  • Hold the paper and the lens in the same position for a short while. Observe what happens.
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

The paper begins to smoke and rapidly catches fire! The convex lens converges all parallel sun rays to a single intense point on the principal axis: the Principal Focus (F2). The concentrated solar radiant energy raises the local temperature above the paper's kindling point.

💡 Key Takeaway: The sharp, bright spot is a real, point-sized image of the Sun. The distance from the lens to the spot gives the focal length (f) of the convex lens.

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.12: Converging Action of Convex Lens & Diverging Action of Concave Lens (Page 151)

  • 🔹 Convex Lens (Converging) [Fig. 9.12(a)]: Bounded by two spherical surfaces bulging outward at the middle; thicker in the middle than at the edges. Gathers parallel incident rays to a real focus F2 on the opposite side.
  • 🔹 Concave Lens (Diverging) [Fig. 9.12(b)]: Bounded by two spherical surfaces curved inward; thicker at the edges than in the middle. Spreads parallel incident rays outward away from a virtual focus F1 on the incident side.
  • 🔹 Two Foci Concept: Because a lens has two spherical refracting surfaces, it possesses two centres of curvature (2F1, 2F2) and two principal foci (F1, F2).

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 151):

"Fig. 9.12 — (a) Converging action of a convex lens, (b) diverging action of a concave lens."

🖼️ Fig. 9.12 – Converging Action of Convex Lens & Diverging Action of Concave Lens

📖 Source: NCERT Page 151

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.12 • Converging Action of Convex Lens & Diverging Action of Concave Lens

Q1: Why is a convex lens called a converging lens while a concave lens is called a diverging lens?

✅ Answer A convex lens converges parallel incoming rays inwards to a common focus point. A concave lens diverges parallel incoming rays outwards away from the principal axis.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (0.5M convex converging + 0.5M concave diverging)

Q2: What is the Optical Centre (O) of a spherical lens?

✅ Answer The Optical Centre (O) is the central point on the principal axis of the lens. Any light ray passing through the optical centre emerges completely undeviated.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Central point where rays pass without deviation)

Q3: Why does a lens have two principal foci, whereas a spherical mirror has only one?

✅ Answer Because a lens has two refracting spherical surfaces through which light can enter from either the left or the right, whereas a mirror has only one active reflecting face.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Two refracting surfaces allowing light entry from either side)

9.18 Canonical Rules for Ray Tracing Through Lenses (Pages 153–154)

Just as with spherical mirrors, we can trace image positions in spherical lenses by following the geometry of any two of the following three standard rays:

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.13: Lens Ray Tracing Rule 1: Ray Parallel to Principal Axis (Page 153)

  • 🔹 Convex Lens Parallel Ray [Fig. 9.13(a)]: A ray from the object parallel to the principal axis refracts through the lens and passes directly through principal focus F2 on the opposite side.
  • 🔹 Concave Lens Parallel Ray [Fig. 9.13(b)]: A ray parallel to the principal axis refracts outward such that it appears to diverge from principal focus F1 on the incident side.
  • 🔹 Focus Selection Rule: Convex converges light to F2 on the far side; concave diverges light as if radiating from F1 on the near side.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 153):

"Fig. 9.13 — Path of a ray parallel to the principal axis: (a) Convex lens, (b) Concave lens."

🖼️ Fig. 9.13 – Lens Ray Tracing Rule 1: Ray Parallel to Principal Axis

📖 Source: NCERT Page 153

📊 Diagram-Based Questions: Fig. 9.13 • Lens Ray Tracing Rule 1: Ray Parallel to Principal Axis

Q1: Where does a ray parallel to the principal axis go after passing through a convex lens?

✅ Answer It refracts through the lens and passes directly through the principal focus (F2) on the other side.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Passes through focus F2 on the other side)

Q2: How does a parallel ray behave after refraction through a concave lens?

✅ Answer It refracts outwards such that it appears to diverge from the principal focus (F1) on the same side as the incident light.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Appears to diverge from focus F1 on the same side)

Q3: What is the optical difference between F1 and F2 for a convex lens?

✅ Answer F1 is the first principal focus on the incident side; F2 is the second principal focus on the emergence side where parallel incident rays converge.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (F1 on incident side, F2 on refraction side)

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.14: Lens Ray Tracing Rule 2: Ray Passing Through Focus (Page 154)

  • 🔹 Convex Lens Focal Ray [Fig. 9.14(a)]: A ray passing through the first principal focus F1 refracts and emerges parallel to the principal axis.
  • 🔹 Concave Lens Focal Ray [Fig. 9.14(b)]: A ray directed towards the second principal focus F2 on the other side refracts and emerges parallel to the principal axis.
  • 🔹 Reversibility of Light: Rule 2 is the exact optical inverse of Rule 1; reversing the path of light produces the exact same geometrical trajectory.

📌 Verbatim Caption (Page 154):

"Fig. 9.14 — Path of a ray passing through or directed towards the focus: (a) Convex lens, (b) Concave lens."

Q1: What direction does a ray take after refraction if it passes through the focus F1 of a convex lens?

✅ Answer It emerges parallel to the principal axis.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Emerges parallel to principal axis)

Q2: Why does this rule represent the optical inverse of Rule 1?

✅ Answer By the Principle of Reversibility of Light, light rays retrace their exact trajectory if the direction of travel is inverted.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Principle of reversibility of light)

Q3: In a concave lens, where must an incident ray be aimed in order to emerge parallel to the axis?

✅ Answer It must be directed towards the principal focus F2 on the opposite side of the lens.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Directed towards focus F2 on other side)

📖 Understanding Fig. 9.15: Lens Ray Tracing Rule 3: Ray Passing Through Optical Centre (Page 154)

  • 🔹 Zero Deviation at Optical Centre: A ray of light passing through the optical centre (O) of a lens emerges without any deviation whatsoever.
  • 🔹 Applicable to Both Lens Types: This undeviated transmission holds strictly true for both thin convex lenses and thin concave lenses.
  • 🔹 Thin Lens Approximation: Near the optical centre, the opposite faces of a thin lens act like a parallel-faced plate of negligible thickness, so lateral shift is essentially zero.

Q1: What happens to a ray of light that passes through the optical centre of a lens?

✅ Answer The ray passes straight through the lens without undergoing any deviation.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Emerges without any deviation)

Q2: Does this zero-deviation rule depend on whether the lens is convex or concave?

✅ Answer No. The rule applies identically to both convex and concave spherical lenses.

Q3: Why is lateral displacement negligible for rays passing through the optical centre of a thin lens?

✅ Answer Because the lens is assumed to be infinitesimally thin, the lateral shift produced between parallel surfaces approaches zero.

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.12 • Image Formation by a Convex Lens Across 6 Positions (NCERT Page 152)

  • Take a convex lens of known focal length (f ≈ 15 cm).
  • Draw a long straight line on a tabletop. Mark points O, F1, 2F1 on the left, and F2, 2F2 on the right such that OF1 = F1(2F1) = OF2 = F2(2F2) = f.
  • Place a burning candle at infinity, beyond 2F1, at 2F1, between F1 and 2F1, at F1, and between F1 and O.
  • Adjust a paper screen on the other side to catch the sharpest image. Note its position, size, and whether inverted or erect.
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

A real, inverted image is captured on the screen for all positions outside F1. When the candle is moved at 2F1, the image is formed exactly at 2F2 with the same size. When placed between F1 and O, no screen image is formed; looking through the lens reveals an enlarged, virtual, and erect image on the same side (magnifying glass effect!).

💡 Key Takeaway: A convex lens forms real, inverted images for 5 positions, and a virtual, erect, magnified image for 1 position.

🔍 ACTIVITY 9.13 • Image Formation by a Concave Lens (NCERT Page 153)

  • Take a concave lens. Place a burning candle in front of it on an optical bench.
  • Attempt to obtain a sharp image of the flame on a screen placed on the other side of the lens. Did you succeed?
  • Now look through the concave lens from the other side. What do you see?
  • Move the candle farther away and note the changes in image position and size.
🔬 Observation & Conclusion:

No image can ever be formed on a screen! Looking through the concave lens always reveals a diminished, erect, and virtual image formed between the optical centre O and focus F1 on the same side as the candle. As the candle moves farther, the image shrinks towards point size at focus F1.

💡 Key Takeaway: A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, and diminished image, regardless of object distance!

🔑 Key Technical Terms & Definitions • Section 5 ▼
Spherical Lens Convex Lens Concave Lens Optical Centre (O) Principal Focus of Lens Focal Length of Lens
  • Spherical Lens: A transparent optical medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which is spherical.
  • Convex Lens: A lens thicker at the centre than at the edges that converges parallel incident rays to a real focus (converging lens).
  • Concave Lens: A lens thicker at the edges than at the centre that diverges parallel incident rays away from a virtual focus (diverging lens).
  • Optical Centre (O): The geometric midpoint of a thin spherical lens through which light rays pass without deviation.
  • Principal Focus of Lens: The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis converge (convex) or appear to diverge from (concave) after refraction.
  • Focal Length of Lens: The linear distance between the Optical Centre (O) and the Principal Focus (F) of the lens.

❓ Q1 (MCQ): A convex lens of focal length 25 cm forms a real image of the same size as the object. The distance of the object from the lens is:
(a) 25 cm   (b) 50 cm   (c) 75 cm   (d) infinity
✅ Answer (b) 50 cm
Explanation: A convex lens forms a real image of the same size when the object is placed at 2F1. Here u = 2f = 2 × 25 = 50 cm.
❓ Q2 (True/False): A ray of light passing through the optical centre of a thick or thin lens always bends towards the base.
✅ Answer False.
Explanation: By optical definition, a ray passing through the Optical Centre (O) emerges without any deviation.
❓ Q3 (Fill in the blank): To use a convex lens as a simple magnifying glass, the object must be placed between the focus F1 and _______.
✅ Answer Optical Centre (O).
Explanation: Only when placed within the focal length (between F1 and O) does a convex lens produce an erect, enlarged virtual image.

9.21 New Cartesian Sign Convention for Spherical Lenses (Pages 155–156)

For lenses, we follow sign conventions identical in geometric spirit to those used for spherical mirrors, with one key distinction: all measurements are taken from the Optical Centre (O) of the lens.

  • The focal length of a convex lens is always POSITIVE (+).
  • The focal length of a concave lens is always NEGATIVE (−).
  • The object distance u is always negative (−) for real objects.
📐

9.22 The Lens Formula & Magnification (Pages 156–157)

This formula gives the relationship between the object distance (u), image distance (v), and focal length (f) of a spherical lens:

🌟 The Lens Formula:

1/v - 1/u = 1/f

⚖️ Critical Formula Comparison: Mirror vs. Lens

Parameter Spherical Mirror Spherical Lens
Fundamental Formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f  (PLUS sign) 1/v - 1/u = 1/f  (MINUS sign)
Linear Magnification (m) m = h'/h = - v / u  (MINUS sign) m = h'/h = + v / u  (PLUS sign)

📐 NCERT Solved Example 9.3 (Page 156) (Page 156)

A concave lens has focal length of 15 cm. At what distance should the object from the lens be placed so that it forms an image at 10 cm from the lens? Also, find the magnification produced by the lens.
📝 Step-by-Step Solution:
1. Given Quantities with Cartesian Signs:
A concave lens always forms a virtual, erect image on the same side as the object.
Image distance, v = -10 cm
Focal length, f = -15 cm (Concave lens has negative focal length)
Object distance, u = ?
Magnification, m = ?
2. Apply the Lens Formula:
1/v - 1/u = 1/f  ⇒  1/u = 1/v - 1/f
3. Substitute Numerical Values:
1/u = 1/(-10) - 1/(-15) = -1/10 + 1/15
Take LCM of 10 and 15 (= 30):
1/u = (-3 + 2) / 30 = -1 / 30
u = -30 cm
4. Calculate Magnification (m):
m = v / u = (-10 cm) / (-30 cm) = +1/3 ≈ +0.33
🎯 Final Result: Object must be placed at 30 cm in front of the lens (u = -30 cm). The magnification is +0.33 (image is erect, virtual, and one-third of the object size).
✅ Verification: A concave lens always yields a negative object distance (u = -30 cm) and a positive fractional magnification (m = +0.33). Perfectly verified! ✓

📐 NCERT Solved Example 9.4 (Pages 156–157) (Page 156–157)

A 2.0 cm tall object is placed perpendicular to the principal axis of a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. The distance of the object from the lens is 15 cm. Find the nature, position and size of the image. Also find its magnification.
📝 Step-by-Step Solution:
1. Given Quantities with Cartesian Signs:
Height of object, h = +2.0 cm
Focal length, f = +10 cm (Convex lens has positive focal length)
Object distance, u = -15 cm
Image distance, v = ?
Height of image, h' = ?
Magnification, m = ?
2. Apply the Lens Formula:
1/v - 1/u = 1/f  ⇒  1/v = 1/f + 1/u
3. Substitute Numerical Values:
1/v = 1/(+10) + 1/(-15) = 1/10 - 1/15
Take LCM of 10 and 15 (= 30):
1/v = (3 - 2) / 30 = +1 / 30
v = +30 cm
4. Calculate Image Height (h') and Magnification:
m = h' / h = v / u  ⇒  h' = h × (v / u)
h' = (+2.0 cm) × [ (+30 cm) / (-15 cm) ] = (+2.0) × (-2) = -4.0 cm
m = v / u = (+30) / (-15) = -2
🎯 Final Result: The image is formed at +30 cm on the other side of the lens. It is real, inverted, 4.0 cm tall (two times enlarged, m = -2).
✅ Verification: Object lies between F1 (10 cm) and 2F1 (20 cm). Theory predicts real, inverted image beyond 2F2 (> 20 cm) and magnified. Here v = +30 cm, m = -2, perfectly confirmed! ✓
⚡

9.23 Power of a Lens & Optical Combinations (Pages 157–158)

The ability of a lens to converge or diverge light rays depends directly on its focal length. For instance, a convex lens of short focal length bends rays through large angles, focusing them very close to the optical centre. The degree of convergence or divergence achieved by a lens is expressed in terms of its optical power.

🌟 Formula for Power of a Lens:

P = 1 / f (in metres)

The SI unit of power of a lens is dioptre (D). 1 D = 1 m-1.

+ Convex Lens: Power is POSITIVE (+)
− Concave Lens: Power is NEGATIVE (−)

💡 More to Know — Optical Lens Combinations:

Many optical instruments (cameras, compound microscopes, astronomical telescopes) combine multiple lenses placed in contact to increase magnification and correct optical aberrations (defects in image sharpness and color fringing). The net optical power P of lenses placed in contact is the simple algebraic sum:

P = P1 + P2 + P3 + ...

Clinical Example: If an optician combines lenses of power +2.0 D and +0.25 D in a spectacle trial frame, the patient experiences an equivalent single lens of power P = +2.0 + 0.25 = +2.25 D.

❓

9.24 In-Text Questions • NCERT Page 158 (Complete Verbatim Solutions)

📌 In-Text Question 1 (Page 158)

Define 1 dioptre of power of a lens.

✅ Answer

1 dioptre (1 D) is defined as the optical power of a lens whose focal length is exactly 1 metre.

1 D = 1 m-1

A convex lens of focal length +1 m has a power of +1 D, whereas a concave lens of focal length -1 m has a power of -1 D.

📌 Marking Scheme: 1 mark - (Power of lens whose focal length is 1 metre; 1 D = 1 m^-1)
📌 In-Text Question 2 (Page 158)

A convex lens forms a real and inverted image of a needle at a distance of 50 cm from it. Where is the needle placed in front of the convex lens if the image is equal to the size of the object? Also, find the power of the lens.

✅ Answer

Part 1 • Location of Needle:

A convex lens forms a real image of the same size as the object only when the object is placed at 2F1 and the image is formed at 2F2.

  • Image distance, v = +50 cm (real image)
  • Since image is at 2F2: 2f = 50 cm  ⇒  f = 50 / 2 = +25 cm = +0.25 m
  • Object distance must be at 2F1: u = -50 cm.

Answer (Part 1): The needle is placed at a distance of 50 cm in front of the convex lens (u = -50 cm).

Part 2 • Power of the Lens:

f = +0.25 m

P = 1 / f = 1 / (+0.25) = +4.0 D

Answer (Part 2): The power of the lens is +4.0 D.

📌 Marking Scheme: 3 marks - (Needle position u = -50 cm 1.5M + Power P = +4 D with positive sign and dioptre unit 1.5M)
📌 In-Text Question 3 (Page 158)

Find the power of a concave lens of focal length 2 m.

✅ Answer

Given:

For a concave lens, focal length is negative: f = -2 m.

Formula: P = 1 / f (in metres)

Calculation:
P = 1 / (-2 m) = -0.5 D

Answer: The power of the concave lens is -0.5 D.

📌 Marking Scheme: 2 marks - (Correct sign f = -2 m 1M + Power P = -0.5 D 1M)
📋

9.25 What You Have Learnt • Master Chapter Summary (NCERT pp. 158–159)

  • Light travels along straight lines in a uniform medium (rectilinear propagation).
  • Mirrors and lenses form real or virtual images depending on object distance.
  • Reflecting surfaces obey the laws of reflection; refracting surfaces obey the laws of refraction.
  • New Cartesian Sign Conventions: distances measured in the direction of incident light are positive; opposite are negative.
  • Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f connects object distance u, image distance v, and focal length f.
  • Focal length of a spherical mirror is half of its radius of curvature: f = R / 2.
  • Magnification by mirror: m = h'/h = -v/u.
  • Light travelling obliquely from rarer to denser medium bends towards the normal; from denser to rarer medium bends away.
  • Snell's Law: sin i / sin r = constant = n21.
  • Absolute refractive index: n = c / v.
  • Lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.
  • Magnification by lens: m = h'/h = +v/u.
  • Power of a lens: P = 1 / f (in metres); unit is dioptre (D).
🔑 Key Technical Terms & Definitions • Section 6 ▼
Lens Formula Linear Magnification (Lens) Power of a Lens (P) Dioptre (D) Lens Combination Power
  • Lens Formula: The fundamental relationship connecting object distance u, image distance v, and focal length f of a lens: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f.
  • Linear Magnification (Lens): The ratio of image height to object height, given by m = h'/h = +v/u for spherical lenses.
  • Power of a Lens (P): The degree of convergence or divergence of light rays achieved by a lens, defined as the reciprocal of its focal length in metres: P = 1/f.
  • Dioptre (D): The SI unit of optical power of a lens; 1 D is the power of a lens of focal length 1 metre (1 D = 1 m^-1).
  • Lens Combination Power: The net power of several thin lenses placed in contact, calculated as the algebraic sum of individual powers: P = P1 + P2 + P3 + ...
📝

Topic 6 Quick Concept Check

❓ Q1 (MCQ): A convex lens has a focal length of 50 cm. Its power in dioptres is:
(a) +0.5 D   (b) +2.0 D   (c) -2.0 D   (d) +5.0 D
✅ Answer (b) +2.0 D
Explanation: First convert focal length to metres: f = +50 cm = +0.50 m. Power P = 1 / f = 1 / (+0.50) = +2.0 D.
❓ Q2 (True/False): If two thin lenses of powers +3.5 D and -1.5 D are held in contact, the combination acts as a converging lens.
✅ Answer True.
Explanation: Net power P = P1 + P2 = +3.5 D + (-1.5 D) = +2.0 D. Since net power is positive (+), the combination behaves as a converging (convex) lens of focal length f = 1 / 2.0 = +0.5 m = +50 cm.
❓ Q3 (Fill in the blank): The SI unit of power of a lens is dioptre, where 1 dioptre = _______.
✅ Answer 1 m-1 (one per metre).
Explanation: Since power is the reciprocal of focal length in metres (P = 1/f), its dimensional unit is m-1.
